source: Misuraca et al. (2024) Frontiers in Psychology, review of choice overload moderators (49 articles)
finding: Review of 49 peer-reviewed papers on what moderates choice overload. Two groups: choice environment and decision-maker traits. Overload is conditional, not universal.
numbers: 49 articles included; moderators: set complexity, task difficulty, brand names, decision goal, preference uncertainty, affect, maximizing, age, culture.
quote: Choice overload has been replicated in numerous fields and laboratory settings
limits: Qualitative review, not a meta-analysis. Says the 2015 meta-analysis found overload only under certain conditions.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a fixed 'too many options' penalty. Condition any option-pruning step on set complexity and whether a dominant option exists.

source: Iyengar and Lepper (2000) jam study, as reported in Misuraca et al. 2024
finding: Jam booth: 24 jams drew more stoppers but far fewer buyers than 6 jams. Satisfaction was lower after choosing from the large set.
numbers: 60% of passers-by stopped at 24 jams vs 40% at 6 jams. Of stoppers, 3% bought at 24 jams vs 30% at 6 jams.
limits: Second-hand numbers from the 2024 review; the original paper was not opened. Later meta-analyses found the average effect near zero (see b04).
agent_relevance: Founding result for 'less is more' in choice. Treat as a hypothesis about when more candidates hurt, not a law.

source: Iyengar and Lepper (2000) essay and chocolate studies; Iyengar et al. (2004) 401(k) data, as reported in Misuraca et al. 2024
finding: Essay topics: fewer choices gave more completed, better essays. Chocolates: fewer choices gave higher satisfaction. 401(k): participation fell as fund count rose.
numbers: Essay: 74% turned in with 6 topics vs 60% with 30 topics. Chocolates: 6 vs 30 options, small set more satisfied. 401(k): 800,000 employees, plans with 2 to 59 funds; participation highest under 10 funds, lowest at 59.
limits: Second-hand. Natural-data 401(k) result is correlational. Original papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports a ceiling on useful branching width. Cap the number of candidates the agent compares at once.

source: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder and Todd (2010) Can there ever be too many options? Meta-analysis, J Consumer Research 37(3):409-425
finding: Meta-analysis found the average choice overload effect was virtually zero, with large differences between studies. Several preconditions were found but no sufficient conditions.
numbers: 63 conditions from 50 experiments; 5,036 participants. Mean d reported as virtually zero (numeric d not on the page I read).
limits: Only the abstract page was read, not the full paper.
agent_relevance: The main failed-replication-style result. The 'paradox of choice' is not a robust main effect, so do not hard-code a small-set rule.

source: Misuraca et al. 2024 review, on the Chernev, Bockenholt and Goodman (2015) meta-analysis and Scheibehenne (2010) preconditions
finding: Review reports that overload depends on four moderator families: set complexity, task difficulty, preference uncertainty, decision goal. An ideal option in the set can offset set size.
numbers: Overload grows with number of attributes and when no option dominates. Experts: overload with small sets, not large (Mogilner 2008, Morrin 2012). Choosing an assortment, or browsing, shows less overload.
quote: the benefits of having an ideal item in the set might compensate for the costs of overwhelming set size
limits: Second-hand summary of the meta-analysis; Chernev 2015 full text returned 403 and was not opened. No effect sizes obtained.
agent_relevance: Gate on whether a clear dominant candidate exists (S0 gate). With a dominant option, large sets are fine; with none, narrow first.

source: Misuraca et al. 2024 review: moderators from Mogilner 2008, Levav 2010, Townsend and Kahn 2014, Polman 2012
finding: Interventions that reduce overload: group options into categories (even meaningless labels), show small sets before large ones, verbal rather than visual for large sets, brand names present, choosing for others.
numbers: Categories A, B... worked as well as meaningful categories (Mogilner 2008). Small-then-large order reduced overload (Levav 2010). Choosing for others: larger set gave more satisfaction (Polman 2012).
limits: Second-hand. Single-study moderators, mostly not independently replicated in the review.
agent_relevance: Chunking candidates into labelled groups is a cheap way to cut load before comparing.

source: Misuraca et al. 2024 review: maximizers vs satisficers, citing Iyengar, Wells and Schwartz (2006) job search
finding: Maximizer graduating students took jobs with about 20% higher salary but felt less satisfied and happy, and more regretful, stressed and anxious, than satisficers.
numbers: Salary about 20% higher for maximizers. Maximizers lower on satisfaction and happiness.
limits: Second-hand from the review. Salary effect is a correlation from a self-selected trait split.
agent_relevance: Maximizing can raise outcome quality and still cost more effort and regret. For an agent the cost is tokens and time, so the stopping rule must price the search.

source: Misuraca et al. 2024 review: age and culture moderators
finding: Adolescents and adults show most overload; children and seniors show less. Eastern Europeans were more satisfied with larger sets than Western Europeans.
numbers: Seniors lean toward satisficing (Tanius 2009). Culture effect from Reutskaja et al. 2022.
limits: Review says most overload work is in Western, individualist samples. Cross-cultural replication is thin.
agent_relevance: Individual and population differences in stopping style are real; one fixed threshold will not fit all tasks.

source: Peng et al. (2018) A new look at the impact of maximizing on unhappiness. Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Maximizing relates to lower life satisfaction through regret, but a second path through hope for success partly offsets it.
numbers: N=395 valid of 402 Chinese undergraduates. Maximizing with regret r=0.45; with life satisfaction r=-0.24; with positive affect r=-0.22; with negative affect r=0.21; with hope for success r=0.13; with fear of failure r=0.08 (ns). Maximization Scale alpha=0.71.
limits: Cross-sectional self-report, one Chinese university sample. Mediation not causal.
agent_relevance: Regret is the cost channel of maximizing; the agent analogue is rework and second-guessing after a good-enough answer exists.

source: Li, Jia and Wang (2023) Maximizing tendency predicts university adjustment and academic performance. Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Counter to the unhappy-maximizer story, maximizing at entry predicted better adjustment and later GPA in two time-lagged studies.
numbers: Study 1: N=552 first-year students (4 Chinese universities), beta=0.11 for adjustment (p=0.016), beta=0.20 for eudaimonic well-being. Study 2: N=309, over 4 years, beta=0.17 for adjustment, beta=0.08 for GPA (p<0.05). R2 0.03 and 0.09.
limits: Small effects, self-report, one country. Uses the 9-item Diab scale, so it is not directly comparable with the 13-item Schwartz scale.
agent_relevance: Maximizing is not uniformly bad. Gains show up where effort pays back, such as exams; bounded search is the right default only when the cost of extra search is high.

source: Oren, Dar and Liberman (2018) Obsessive-compulsive tendencies are related to a maximization strategy. Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Obsessive-compulsive tendencies track maximizing even after controlling for indecisiveness, depression and anxiety. Reliance on external proxies partly explains the link.
numbers: Study 1: N=201 Hebrew-speaking adults. Study 2: N=240 English-speaking adults, plus a hypothetical decision scenario.
limits: Unscreened online samples; correlational; exact coefficients not extracted.
agent_relevance: Maximizing as a pathology of verification: an agent that cannot stop checking shows the failure the S0 gate and G11/G12 stopping rules guard against.

source: Shortland, Thompson and Alison (2020) Police perfection: trait maximization and police decision-making. Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Among senior UK police officers, maximizers found emergency decisions harder. Military experience sped up committing to a course of action.
numbers: n=96 senior police officers. Maximization correlated with decision difficulty r=0.249 (p=0.014), with Need for Closure r=0.339 (p=0.001). Maximization score M=120.54, SD=16.97 on the 34-item inventory.
limits: Expert sample but scenario-based; no outcome-quality measure (the authors say they do not identify better decision-makers).
agent_relevance: Expert, high-stakes users still show a cost of maximizing; experience moderates how fast they commit.

source: Tejeiro et al. (2026) Validation of the Maximizing Tendency Scale in a Spanish nursing population
finding: The short 7-item Maximizing Tendency Scale held up in a new language and occupation, with one factor.
numbers: N=213 nurses (83.5% female). Cronbach alpha 0.78; 2-week test-retest r=0.89; ICC 0.78. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis both gave one factor.
limits: Abstract-level numbers; one province. Notes that up to 13 competing maximization scales exist, a measurement-validity problem for the whole literature.
agent_relevance: Measures of 'maximizer' differ by scale; results in b09 to b12 are not interchangeable.

source: Seo, Lee, Lee and Kim (2026) Reducing cognitive demand fails to mitigate choice overload: multimodal neural and gaze evidence for effort conservation
finding: Two experiments with eye tracking and EEG: making choices easier (high-attractiveness sets, or a bookmark shortlist) sped decisions but did not improve choice quality as set size grew. People conserved effort rather than reallocating it.
numbers: Set sizes 6 to 24. E1 N=17, E2 N=28 analysed. Decisions faster: 5.85 vs 7.38 s (E1), 5.47 vs 6.30 s (E2). Screening ratio 0.69 vs 0.81 (E1) and 0.69 vs 0.77 (E2). Performance lower under low demand: F(1,16)=13.66, p=0.002, partial eta2=0.46. Demand x set size F(3,48)=11.89, partial eta2=0.43.
quote: simplifying decisions can backfire: when choices feel easier, people disengage rather than optimize
limits: Very small samples, university students, movie-poster task, one lab.
agent_relevance: Shortlisting by itself can lower final quality because the chooser stops searching earlier. A pruning step needs a check on what was dropped.

source: Chehade et al. (2025) Bounded rationality for LLMs: satisficing alignment at inference time (SITAlign), ICML 2025, arXiv 2505.23729
finding: Maximize one main objective at decoding time and treat the others as thresholds to clear. Beat a prior multi-objective decoder in GPT-4 judged win-tie rate.
numbers: Helpfulness win-tie +22.3% over MOD on PKU-SafeRLHF-30K (Zephyr-7B-beta). About +10% on Anthropic-HH with humor threshold (MPT-7B-Chat). Third setting: summarization with faithfulness (Minotaur-7B). Thresholds beta=-12 and beta=-0.5 give a 50% win-tie constraint. Over 90% of responses with reward at least -12 were judged harmless. Top-k=10; 20 sampled responses per prompt in the proof of concept.
quote: SITAlign outperforms the state-of-the-art multi-objective decoding strategy by a margin of 22.3%
limits: Judged by GPT-4, not humans. The 22.3% is not clearly absolute or relative. No best-of-N baseline and no test of reward overoptimization. Threshold setting needs GPT-4 win rates or human feedback. One attribute checked closely (harmlessness).
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of satisficing: thresholds for secondary criteria instead of maximizing all. Matches G11/G12 stopping, but the threshold has to be calibrated on data.

source: Chehade et al. (2025) SITAlign threshold ablation (Figure 3)
finding: Raising the secondary-objective threshold raises that objective's win-tie rate, then plateaus while the main objective keeps dropping.
numbers: Values only in plots, not in text. Theory: suboptimality gap grows with threshold strictness (beta_1, beta_max).
limits: Numbers only in plots. Stated limits: conservative policy at large alpha or beta_1; KL divergence rises at small values.
agent_relevance: A satisficing threshold has an interior optimum. Set it by checking the plateau, not by maximal strictness.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs, arXiv 2412.21187
finding: Reasoning models spend many tokens on easy problems and keep checking after the first right answer. Training for shorter outputs cut tokens with small accuracy change.
numbers: o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models on 2+3. First round already correct in over 92% of cases. QwQ example: 13 solutions, 7 distinct, 901 tokens. Baseline QwQ MATH500: 93.0% acc, 2407.9 tokens, outcome efficiency 52.3%. SimPO FCS+Reflection: MATH500 93.0 to 92.8 acc, tokens 2407.9 to 1330.7 (-44.7%); GSM8K 94.8 to 96.0, -46.1%; AIME24 46.7 to 43.3, -45.6%; GPQA 59.6 to 59.1, -35.4%.
limits: Models: QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1. Intro cites 48.6% on MATH500 but the table gives 48.6% for ASDIV; MATH500 is 44.7%. Reduction numbers are arithmetic from the table. Read through a summarizing fetch tool, not the raw PDF.
agent_relevance: Quantifies a missing stopping rule: first correct answer is usually enough. Cheap argument for an explicit satisficing stop after a verified answer.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic early exit in reasoning models, arXiv 2504.15895
finding: A training-free rule stops a model's own chain of thought early when it is confident in a trial answer at a reasoning transition point.
numbers: 10 benchmarks, 11 reasoning LLMs. Chain-of-thought length cut 19.1% to 80.1% on average, with accuracy up 0.3% to 5.0%.
limits: Abstract page only. Per-model and per-benchmark values not read.
agent_relevance: A working confidence-triggered satisficing stop for LLM reasoning, with no accuracy loss on average.

source: Liu, Geng, Peterson, Sucholutsky and Griffiths (2024) LLMs assume people are more rational than we really are, arXiv 2406.17055
finding: LLMs predict human gambling choices as if people maximized expected value. With chain-of-thought they match expected value better than humans do.
numbers: choices13k: 9,831 of 13,006 problems used. Spearman with human choices (CoT): GPT-4-Turbo 0.639, GPT-4o 0.611, Llama-3-70B 0.616, Claude 3 Opus 0.576, Llama-3-8B 0.463. Spearman with max expected value (CoT): GPT-4o 0.944, GPT-4-Turbo 0.932; humans 0.484. GPT-4o CoT MSE 0.0278 vs humans 0.2580.
quote: LLMs assume people are more rational than they actually are
limits: Claude 3 Opus run only on first task. Risky gambles, not satisficing in search. A 'monkey prompt' made predictions less rational and closer to human. Last 5,487 characters of the page not read.
agent_relevance: LLMs lean toward maximizing by default; satisficing has to be put in by the scaffold. Do not use model self-prediction of human behavior as a bounded-rationality check.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee and Nguyen (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? GPT-3.5, arXiv 2305.04400
finding: GPT-3.5 showed anchoring, conjunction/availability effects, framing and the endowment effect, as humans did on the same prompts.
numbers: 4 studies, GPT-3.5 only. No sample sizes or effect sizes on the page I read.
limits: Abstract page only. Single early model. Later models may behave differently (see b19 for the shift toward expected value).
agent_relevance: Heuristic-like biases appear in the language model itself; scaffolds should not assume the model is a clean maximizer.

source: Bohnet et al. (2026) Analysis of optimality of LLMs on planning problems, arXiv 2604.02910
finding: Reasoning LLMs beat the classical satisficing planner LAMA on complex multi-goal Blocksworld and path-star graphs, tracking optimal plan limits.
numbers: No figures on the abstract page. Models named only as frontier reasoning models.
limits: Abstract only; no numbers read. The claim of near-perfect optimality needs the full paper.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence: for planning, current LLMs may maximize better than satisficing search, so satisficing is not always the better default.

source: Kang et al. (2026) Human heuristics and strategies in everyday decision-making conversations, CogSci 2026, arXiv 2605.07789
finding: In 955 real Korean conversations about food and travel, people favored satisficing and heuristics. Common heuristics keep talk moving; rarer rule-based strategies are best at reaching a decision.
numbers: 955 conversations, 15,476 utterances, coded with an LLM-assisted pipeline.
limits: Abstract page only. LLM-coded data. Everyday low-stakes domains.
agent_relevance: Human choosers close decisions with a few rule-like moves; conversational agents could use the same closing moves.

source: Reutskaja, Nagel, Camerer and Rangel (2011) Search dynamics in consumer choice under time pressure. American Economic Review 101(2):900-926
finding: Eye-tracking: people optimize well among items they look at, search order is largely random with respect to value, and stopping mixes optimal search and satisficing.
numbers: Abstract only: no sample sizes or conditions read.
limits: Abstract page only; full PDF not opened.
agent_relevance: Evidence that stopping rules in the lab combine a good-enough threshold with a cost of search, not pure Simon satisficing.

source: Czerlinski, Goldstein and Gigerenzer (1999), as summarized on Wikipedia, Take-the-best heuristic
finding: On 83 German cities, simple rules matched regression in fit and beat it slightly out of sample.
numbers: In-sample: regression 74.3%, take-the-best 74.2%, unit-weight 74.1%. Out-of-sample (10,000 random half splits): take-the-best 72.2%, regression 71.9%, unit-weight 71.4%.
limits: Wikipedia page, with figures tagged citation needed; original not opened. Margins under 0.5 points. Binary cues, uncertain environment.
agent_relevance: Less-is-more is real but small; use it to justify cheap rules, not to claim they are better.

source: Keramati, Dezfouli and Piray (2011) Speed/accuracy trade-off between habitual and goal-directed processes. PLoS Comput Biol
finding: A model that trades search time against accuracy explains why choice reaction time rises with the number of options and why behavior becomes habitual with training.
numbers: Model paper. Arbitration picks the fast habit or the slow goal-directed search by weighing value of information against time cost.
limits: Simulations of animal data, not a test with LLMs. Only the abstract and front matter were read closely.
agent_relevance: A formal, resource-rational template for when to stop planning and act: compare expected gain from more search to its time cost.

source: Veldwijk et al. (2023) Taking the shortcut: simplifying heuristics in discrete choice experiments. Patient
finding: Respondents often use simplifying rules (attribute non-attendance, thresholds, lexicographic) that break random-utility assumptions; ignoring them biases preference estimates.
numbers: Review; key point: ignoring heuristics biases parameter estimates and creates false preference heterogeneity. No prevalence figures in the text I read.
limits: Health-economics setting. Qualitative overview.
agent_relevance: Satisficing-like rules are common in real choice data; evaluate an agent on the rule it actually used, not only on the final answer.

source: Spiliopoulos and Ortmann (2018) The BCD of response time analysis in experimental economics. Experimental Economics
finding: Review argues that response time and time-pressure experiments help identify which heuristic people use, and that process models are needed, not outcome models.
numbers: Review; no single effect size. Only the abstract and introduction were read.
limits: Methods paper on economics experiments.
agent_relevance: Method lesson: manipulate time or token budget to reveal the stopping rule rather than inferring it from answers.
